activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
story:
Makayla found the broken axle at 4:37, ten minutes before Coach Dan locked the gym, and by the time she'd carried the robot to the bench everyone else had packed up except Priya, who was still coiling extension cords with the slow precision of someone avoiding a conversation.

The robot was for Saturday. The drive base had failed twice during the scrimmage run, both times on Priya's new mounting bracket, and Makayla had spent the whole practice biting down on the sentence she actually wanted to say, which was some version of you ruined the drive base and now we have three days. She set the robot down on the bench between them.

"I'm not mad," Priya said, which was the wrong opening, because it meant she thought Makayla might be.

"I'm not either." That was mostly true. What Makayla felt was closer to foreboding, a tightening behind her ribs every time she pictured Saturday's first match and the robot tipping over on the ramp in front of two hundred people. She could say that. She was less sure she should.

Priya finished the last cord and sat on her heels. "The bracket was too heavy. I knew when I printed it."

"Then why'd you put it on?"

"Because everyone was so excited that it fit." Priya looked at the floor. "I thought I could fix it during the scrimmage."

There it was, the actual problem, sitting out in the open, and Makayla understood that whatever she said in the next thirty seconds would either make Priya defensive or make her a teammate Makayla could count on in three days. She had watched it go both ways on this team. Last season Dominic had told a freshman his code "was a disaster," honest and specific and completely useless, because the freshman had stopped volunteering for anything after that. Honesty without care had effectively incapacitated him; he'd sat at the parts table for the rest of the season sorting screws. Makayla did not want to do that to Priya. She also did not want to say "it's fine," because it wasn't, and Priya would know she was being managed.

Her psych binder was in her bag, and she remembered the page from Monday, the one she'd half-read while eating lunch. She dug it out and found the heading while Priya watched her, puzzled. The notes said that I-messages, statements like "I felt stuck when the parts came in late," were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise a problem without blaming. She'd written it down thinking it was a worksheet answer, nothing to do with her life.

"I-messages," she said, half to herself, tapping the page. "Gordon, sixties."

"What?"

"Nothing. Give me a second." She tried, silently, the sentence she'd been holding. You put a bad bracket on and now we might lose. She rebuilt it. "I panicked during the scrimmage when the base tipped, because I couldn't tell if it was the bracket or my driving, and I felt like I couldn't say anything without it coming out wrong."

Priya blinked. "It was the bracket. Not your driving. I checked the weight after."

"Okay. Then here's what I need." Makayla pointed at the broken axle. "A bracket under forty grams by Friday, and I'd like to test it with you before we mount it, instead of after. Not because I don't trust you. Because I drive better when I'm not guessing."

"That's fair." Priya picked up the robot and turned it over, studying the mounting plate the way she studied everything, like it owed her an explanation. "I have filament for a lighter print. I can run it tonight."

They walked out together, and in the parking lot Priya stopped by the chain-link gate. "You could have just yelled at me. It would've been faster."

"Probably." Makayla shifted her bag on her shoulder. "But then Friday would be us being weird at each other, and Saturday we'd still have a heavy bracket." She wasn't entirely sure that was true, that kindness had bought them anything besides time. Maybe Priya's new print would fail too. Maybe being this careful was just a slower way of being dishonest, postponing the real conversation until it exploded on the bus to the competition. She held both possibilities at once, and let them stand next to each other, the way the robot and the toolbox stood next to each other in the back of her car.

"Text you when the print's done," Priya said. "Come by at nine if you're awake."

"I'll be awake," Makayla said, and clicked the hatch shut on the robot, the axle, and all three days they had left.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
story:
Mr. Okonkwo's fourth-period environmental science class had a poster on the back wall, a long jagged line climbing like a staircase from left to right, and for the first three weeks of the semester Elliot had never once looked at it. He looked at it now, because the quiz on Friday required him to explain, out loud, in his own words, how greenhouse gases trapped heat, and reading the textbook's version aloud had earned him a look from Mr. Okonkwo that meant try again, in your own head this time.

His lab partner, Dana, spread the handout between them: the same graph from the poster, monthly carbon dioxide measurements from a station on a volcano in Hawaii called Mauna Loa, marching across a century. The line wobbled each year, a small rise and fall, rising and falling, while underneath the wobble it climbed and climbed. "The sawtooth part is seasons," Dana said. "Plants breathe, basically. That I can say on the quiz. The other part, the heat thing, I keep saying it wrong."

Elliot had thought he understood it too, in the vague way he understood most things that everyone repeated. The blanket metaphor. The greenhouse metaphor, which he had privately begun to suspect was the problem, because when he pictured a greenhouse, he pictured glass walls, and there was no glass in the sky, and metaphors that didn't hold up under one question weren't explanations, they were decorations. He said so, and Dana frowned and tapped the graph.

"So what actually happens?" she asked.

He didn't answer right away, which was unusual for him, and he noticed that it was unusual, and that noticing felt like something beginning. He took out his notebook and drew a squiggle. Sunlight comes in, mostly straight through, visible light, short waves. The ground soaks it up, warms, and radiates heat back out as infrared, longer waves. And certain gases, the ones in the graph, are transparent to the short waves coming in and not transparent to the long waves going out, so the outgoing heat gets absorbed and re-radiated, some of it back downward. "It's not a lid," he said slowly. "It's more like the air gets slightly worse at letting go." Dana copied his squiggle, and something about watching her copy it rearranged the idea again in his own mind, the way explaining always did, each telling a slightly different thing than the one before.

That night he video-called his grandfather, mostly because his grandfather had a habit of asking one question too many and Elliot wanted practice being asked. He held the handout up to the camera, the graph filling the little window, his grandfather's face small in the corner, squinting. "There," his grandfather said, pointing, as if he could touch it through the screen. "Where it crosses that line you drew at four hundred. When was that?"

Elliot hadn't drawn the line at four hundred; it was printed there, a faint horizontal guide. He looked. The line crossed it partway up the right side, and he remembered the number they'd been given in class, and the memory arrived with its whole context attached. "May ninth, twenty thirteen," he said. "The daily average at Mauna Loa passed four hundred parts per million that day. First time in the whole record." He heard himself say it and checked it against his notes, because he wanted to be the kind of person who checked. His grandfather was quiet for a moment, and then he said, "I was sixty-one," which was not a question, and Elliot understood that the graph had just become, for his grandfather, a kind of calendar, the way it had been a kind of staircase for him, and that it could be both.

On Friday Mr. Okonkwo called on Dana first, and she did the sawtooth and the seasons and the air getting worse at letting go, her version of Elliot's squiggle, and Elliot listened to it with a strange double feeling, recognizing his own words and not quite owning them anymore. Then it was his turn. He stood, and instead of reaching for the blanket, he reached for the wobble. "You can see the planet breathing," he said, "once a year, every year, in the little dips, and it's been breathing the whole time the line climbs, and it keeps climbing anyway. The breathing never stops it. That's the part that got to me."

He had meant to sound analytical. He heard instead that he sounded like someone slightly enthralled by a graph, and he let that stand, because it was true, and because the alternative, the posture of ironic detachment half his grade had adopted toward everything, had started to feel less like intelligence and more like a costume. Even Marcus, slouched in the back with his insouciant half-smile, had sat forward a little during the breathing part, and Elliot filed that away as data.

Walking out, Dana caught up with him. "So is it fixable?" she asked. "The whole thing. That's the part I can't tell from the graph."

"Neither can I," Elliot said. "The graph doesn't say. It just says where we are." They stood a moment by the poster on the back wall, the staircase going up past the faint line at four hundred, into the part of the paper where the printing stopped and the line kept its own counsel. Dana traced the crossing point with one finger, twice, like checking a door.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
story:
Alyssa stood at the boards with a clipboard she had filled the night before, watching twelve twelve-year-olds swarm the ice in a drill she had designed, and watched it fail. The plan was simple: three lines, a pass to the wing, a shot on net. But every pass skidded along the ice, and every defenseman's stick found it, and the drill collapsed into turnovers and peevish little slashes at shin pads. Two parents in the stands. Coach Reyes, who had handed her the mites for three weeks while he took the varsity to regionals, had said only, "They can't complete a pass through traffic. Fix that," and left.

She blew the whistle. "Gather up." They drifted in, sticks on knees, breathing hard. She crouched over the puck she'd kept and tried to think what a coach would say, what Reyes would say, and instead heard her father, from years ago, in this same rink, when she was seven and crying because her passes kept getting knocked away. "Stop crying and lift it," he'd said, and he'd rolled a puck onto its edge and flipped it across the carpet at home, flat and spinning, over a rolled-up towel. She hadn't understood then. She'd just done it until it worked. "A saucer pass," he'd called it, and that was all he'd said, no more explanation than that, and she'd learned it with her hands before she could have explained it to anyone.

Now she tried to explain it. "Watch." She set the puck, drew it back, and flicked it. The puck rose just off the ice, spinning flat, sailed over the blade of a pylon she'd planted as a defender's stick, and dropped onto the tape of her demonstration winger, Priya, who trapped it cleanly. "It lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over the other team's stick," she said. "It comes down on your blade. That's the whole thing. That's what we're learning today."

Priya frowned. "You always told us to keep it on the ice."

"I did." Alyssa had, all last season, when she was an assistant and passes were going into skates. Keep it flat, keep it simple. That had been her first instinct, and it had been wrong for this team, or at least wrong for this problem, and she didn't try to dress it up. "The ice pass is right when nobody's in the way. When there's a stick in the lane, you need this."

They lined up. The first ten minutes were ugly. Kids torqued their wrists and launched wobbling pucks that helicoptered over the glass, and one clipped the boards near the parents, and Alyssa skated to the far gate to retrieve a puck and heard one father say, loudly enough to be heard, "Nineteen-year-old running technocracy drills out there," and laugh at his own word, and she felt her face go hot and skated back without answering because answering would have been worse.

The drill kept failing and she kept adjusting. Too much lift, she said, means the receiver can't catch it. She moved the pylons closer, so the margin for error shrank, and the passing got worse before it got better, which she had not expected and had to decide to tolerate. She cut one line to shorten the wait. She made the wingers call for the pass early, so the passer looked up before flicking. Small things, one at a time, and she wrote none of them down because she was learning that a drill wasn't a plan on a clipboard, it was something you bent while it was happening.

Then Marcus, the smallest defenseman, who had spent the whole hour maligning the drill, the pylons, the cold, made one. He drew the puck back, opened his blade, and flipped it flat over the stick of Owen, the biggest kid on the team, and it landed square on Priya's tape, and Priya buried it. The rink got quiet for half a second and then the whole line banged sticks on the ice. Marcus skated back to his line with his chin up, already complaining about something else, but his chin was up.

"Again," Alyssa said. "Same thing. Off the wall pass, then the saucer." And it started working, not every time, maybe one in four, then one in three, and she stood at the blue line watching pucks rise just off the ice and come down on blades and thinking about her father's carpet and the rolled towel, and about how he had never explained anything, and about how she had just explained it in two sentences, and about which of them had been right. Maybe he'd been right for a seven-year-old and she was right for twelve-year-olds. Maybe you needed both. She didn't know, and the not knowing didn't stop the drill from running, which was something she was also learning.

At the end of practice she collected pylons. The father who'd made the technocracy joke was waiting by the door with his daughter's bag, and he said, "Saucer pass. Haven't seen one of those in a while. Nice." She said, "Thanks," and kept stacking, and behind her Priya and Marcus were arguing about whether Priya's goal counted since Owen had lifted his stick late, and she let them argue, and carried the last pylon off the ice.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
story:
Alexandre had claimed the corner table by the periodicals at ten in the morning, and by noon he had spread three books on comparative government across it, a stack of printed articles, and a legal pad with two columns ruled down the middle. At the top of the left column he had written parliamentary. At the top of the right, presidential. In eight days he would sit an entrance interview for a politics program in Montreal, and the interviewer, according to the program's website, liked to ask first-year applicants one question: which system would you rather live under, and why. Alexandre did not yet have an answer, and the not having felt like a debt accruing interest.

The parliamentary column filled quickly. He wrote that the head of government was the prime minister, chosen by the legislature itself, and that the same majority could withdraw its confidence and force a resignation or an election. One column of power, flowing in one direction. It was tidy. It made removal almost arithmetic: lose the numbers, lose the office.

The presidential column went worse. He wrote that the president was elected separately from the legislature, for a fixed term, and then he stopped, because he could not remember how such a president was removed, only that there was a word for it, and that the word was used loosely by people on television. He left a blank space and underlined it twice.

A girl about his age slid into the chair across from him without asking. She had a canvas bag with a broken zipper and a paperback of poems held together with a rubber band. "You have the whole table," she said. "The study rooms are booked until four. I need somewhere to rehearse."

"Rehearse what?"

"A reading. Saturday. I'm sharing the bill with two other people and one of them is very loud, so I need to be louder in a different way." She set the paperback down. "I'm Priya. I'll be quiet. Quieter than the loud one, anyway."

He moved two books to make room. She began mouthing her poem, occasionally whispering a line, while he went back to the blank space. On his phone he pulled up the transcript of a courthouse tour he had attended the previous spring with his civics class. He had recorded it because the teacher offered extra credit, and he had never once played it back. He skipped forward through the guide's voice until he reached a question from a student named Elliott, who had asked what happened when a president got impeached. "So when they impeach him, he's out," Elliott had said, "right? Impeachment means he's removed."

Alexandre remembered the moment, because the guide had paused with her hand on the railing of the staircase. "No," she had said. "Impeachment is the accusation. In the United States, the House of Representatives impeaches a president by a simple majority, but the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict and remove them." Elliott had looked briefly belligerent, as though the distinction had been invented on the spot to embarrass him, and then he had written it down.

Alexandre wrote it down now, in the right column, word for word as the recording gave it to him. Then he sat back and looked at the two columns together for the first time. The parliamentary side was a door that opened with one push. The presidential side was a door with two locks, and the second lock needed a much larger key. Two separate bodies, two different thresholds, one for accusing and one for removing. He drew an arrow between the columns and wrote, near it, "stability or accountability?" and immediately crossed out the question mark and wrote the word "tradeoff" instead, because he suspected the interviewer would like that word, and then felt faintly dishonest for suspecting it.

"It's not a poem about government," Priya said, watching him. "In case you're wondering about the overlap."

"Sorry. What's it about?"

"A fish. A fish that might be able to feel everything, and a person who has to decide whether to cook it. There's a word for whether something can feel, did you know that? Sentience. Whether there's somebody home in there." She tapped the paperback. "That's the whole problem of the poem. You can't get an answer out of a fish."

"You ask it a question and it just sits there," Alexandre said.

"Exactly. And you still have to decide about the pan." She went back to whispering, and he went back to his columns, and the parallel of it did not strike him until later, when he was packing up.

He had wanted the blank filled. It was filled now, and the filling had made the whole question harder rather than easier, because he could see the argument on both sides and could not find a lever that tipped one over the other. The parliamentary system removed a head of government whenever a majority lost faith, quick and blunt. The presidential system made removal deliberately difficult, one chamber to accuse by simple majority, another to actually remove, and only with two-thirds willing. He trusted neither absolutely. He wrote a final line on the legal pad, under both columns: "I would rather live where the prime minister answers every day, but I would rather be accused where two chambers have to agree, most of the way, twice." He read it over and could not tell whether it was a position or a hedge, and left it on the page anyway.

At four o'clock Priya closed her paperback and recited the fish poem once at full voice, quietly loud, watching the reference desk to see if the librarian would look up. She didn't. Priya grinned and began restretching the rubber band.

"What's your interview question," she said, "the one you've been fighting all day?"

"Which system I'd rather live under."

"And?"

"I think I'll tell them I know how each one fires its leader, and that I'm still deciding what that's worth."

"Good," Priya said. "Say it exactly like that, and then don't recuperate." She wound the rubber band tight around the book. "The deciding is the good part."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
story:
The packet was on Sara's desk before the bell finished ringing: five pages in Spanish, a rubric, and a note in Ms. Ferrán's looping hand that said only "Sara, día jueves." Thursday. Five minutes, in front of everyone, arguing a current issue entirely in Spanish. She flipped to the rubric and found a row labeled Nivel objetivo: B2. No translation. No mercy.

At lunch she took the packet to Tomás, who had lived in Seville until he was eleven and now ate his sandwiches like a man being timed. "B2," she said, pointing at the row. "What is that?"

"It's from the Common European Framework," he said, mouth full. "It describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options." He swallowed. "So basically you. Supposedly."

"So it's not just talk. It's argue, then admit the other side exists." She said it flatly, testing it.

"That's the whole thing, sí." He went back to his sandwich.

That night her topic sat on the screen of her laptop like a dare: whether the school should switch to a four-day week. She had opinions. She had, in fact, too many opinions, all of them in English, all of them arriving at her tongue at once and dying there. She wrote "recuperar" at the top of her notes, because Tomás had told her that the Spanish for the lost sleep she'd recuperate on a free Friday was recuperar, and she liked the shape of it. Then she wrote nothing else for forty minutes. Her desk lamp buzzed. Her father knocked once, saw her face, and slid a plate of toast through the door without comment, which was its own kind of language.

Wednesday after school she commandeered the empty chemistry lab, which smelled of chalk and something faintly citrus from the janitor's mop bucket, and she made Ana listen. Ana sat on a counter swinging her feet, playing the role of skeptic with an ascetic's discipline: no encouragement, no smiles, just "otra vez" every time Sara stalled. The first run lasted ninety seconds. The second, two minutes. On the third attempt Sara got out "los estudiantes podrían... podrían..." and stopped so long that Ana finally offered, "¿Recuperar el sueño?" like handing her a rope.

"No. Don't rescue me." Sara said it in English, then again in Spanish, slower. "Si me rescátas, nunca aprendo." That was the moment it shifted, though she couldn't have said why. Not fluency. Something more like agreeing to walk out onto a plank in public. She stopped trying to sound like a textbook and started sounding like herself with fewer words, which turned out to be a different self, one who had to choose. In English she could hedge forever. In Spanish she had to pick a side and stand there, holding the disadvantages in her other hand where everyone could see them, because that was the level. That was, she understood now, what B2 meant, not charm but structure: a viewpoint, and the honest weight against it.

Thursday came. Room 114, afternoon light lying in long bars across the linoleum, the radiator ticking like something vestigial from a century that still believed in winter. Ms. Ferrán checked her watch and said "Sara, cuando quieras." Sara stood. The first sentence came out too fast. The second came out right. Somewhere in the third minute she heard herself say that a four-day week would let students recuperar real rest, and then, in the fourth minute, say the thing she'd been afraid of: "Pero existe una desventaja seria," and lay it out, the working parents, the younger kids, the hours that had to come from somewhere. Her hands were shaking. Her voice wasn't.

At four minutes fifty she stopped, one option still unexplained, one advantage she'd planned and never reached. Silence. Ms. Ferrán made a small mark on her clipboard and said, "Bien. ¿Preguntas?" and Rodrigo, from the back, who had spent the whole five minutes slouched like a dismissed hypothesis, raised his hand and asked, in Spanish, what she would say to a student whose parents worked Fridays.

Sara looked at the clock. Six seconds gone already. "Diría que tiene razón," she said, and reached for the next word.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
story:
Sophie had told the health science teacher, Ms. Okafor, that she wasn't nervous about the practical exam, and she had told herself the same thing on the bus, and again in the hallway, which was already twice more than a person usually needs to repeat something true. The exam was simple on paper: take a classmate's blood pressure, get an accurate number, then explain in plain language how diet and exercise could change it over time. Sophie had practiced the cuff until she could wrap it in her sleep. What she hadn't practiced was what happened when the numbers came out wrong.

Her partner was Priya, who wanted the certification for a lifeguarding job that started in June and had already bought the whistle. Priya ran to fourth period from the far portables every day, and today was no different. She dropped into the chair, held out her arm while still catching her breath, and Sophie pumped the cuff the way she'd been taught. The screen flashed a number that made both of them lean closer, a top number high enough that Ms. Okafor would have to note it on the skills sheet.

"That's not me," Priya said. "I mean, that can't be me."

Sophie wrote it down anyway, because the sheet demanded a number, and the number was the number. But she kept looking at Priya's sneakers, one heel tapping the floor, the other tucked under the chair, and at her arm dangling loose in her lap instead of resting on the desk. Something about the posture bothered her, though she couldn't have said why, and she was fairly sure the machines in the nurse's office were too antiquated to trust anyway. She'd half convinced herself the equipment was the whole problem by the time Ms. Okafor paused beside their desk.

"Read it again," Ms. Okafor said, which wasn't an explanation, only an instruction, and then she moved on to the next pair.

Priya complained that she didn't want a number like that in her file, that a bad reading would follow her to the lifeguard job, that people would stigmatize her as the one with the high blood pressure. Sophie said nobody's file said anything of the kind, and privately thought Priya was being dramatic, which was a thought she would later have to revise.

After school they stopped at the pharmacy on Alder Street because Priya wanted a second opinion from the machine by the pharmacy counter, the kind with its own chair and its own printed slip. A man hurried in ahead of them, dropped his bag, sat down and jammed his arm in immediately, still muttering into his phone, and got a number that made him frown and do the whole thing over again. This time he put the phone away, sat back, planted both feet flat on the floor, and set his arm on the machine's rest so it sat level with his heart. He waited. The second slip printed, and the top number was much lower than the first, low enough that he folded both slips together, pocketed them, and left looking relieved.

Sophie read the instruction card mounted beside the machine, the one nobody ever read, including the man, who had done it by second nature. For an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers. She stood there holding the card's edge while Priya paid for lip balm.

"You ran to class," Sophie said. "You were still breathing hard. And your arm wasn't supported, and your feet weren't flat, and we didn't wait." She said it slowly, testing each part against what she'd seen. "Posture and activity change the numbers. So we measured the run, not you."

Priya sat down in the machine's chair, put her phone in her pocket, and set a timer for five minutes. She kept her feet flat and her arm on the rest at heart level, and for the whole five minutes she was quiet, which Sophie had never once witnessed before. The machine inflated, deflated, printed. The number was lower, ordinary, unremarkable. Priya tore off the slip and held it up to the light like a ticket she'd won.

The next morning Sophie asked Ms. Okafor to recheck the practical. She took Priya's reading after a quiet stretch of the period, feet flat, arm supported, and then talked her way through the second half of the exam, how weeks of walking and a diet lower in salt could bring the numbers down over time, how the reading was a snapshot and not a verdict. Ms. Okafor made a small mark on the sheet and said the retake would be Monday. Sophie walked out to the portables telling herself she had never been nervous in the first place, and rehearsing, under her breath, "five minutes, feet flat, arm at heart level," as Priya jogged past her toward class.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
story:
The training binder had a sticker of a cartoon condom on the front, which Amelia took as the program's first statement of philosophy: if you could survive the embarrassment of the sticker, you could survive anything. She had signed up to be a peer health educator mostly because the alternative was study hall, but by the third Tuesday session she had found that she liked the material, liked the strange dignity of words like "contraception" spoken out loud in a classroom, liked the way her grandmother's brisk caution and the nurse practitioner's unhurried factuality could both be true at once. Her grandmother believed knowledge of such things invited trouble; the trainer believed ignorance invited it faster. Amelia had not yet decided which half of her inheritance to amortize over the rest of her life, so for now she paid attention to both.

The trouble, when it arrived, arrived by text. Priya, from her chemistry class, sent a single message at 9:47 on a Thursday night: can i call. Not a question mark in sight, which was how Amelia knew it was serious.

Priya's voice on the phone was querulous in a way Priya never was, all edges and small grievances stacked on top of one larger unspoken thing. The condom broke. It had broken Saturday night, which Amelia made her say twice, because her first instinct was to believe she had misheard the timeline. Saturday. Five days ago. Priya had spent the intervening days telling herself that stress had delayed her period, that the odds were small, that waiting was the mature option, that a pharmacy would judge her, that she would figure it out tomorrow.

"Okay," Amelia said, pulling on shoes with the phone wedged against her shoulder. "We're going to find a pharmacy that's open late. Right now. I'm looking."

"Do you actually know anything about this," Priya said, "or are you just being brave at me?"

"Both are happening simultaneously."

The pharmacist was a compact woman named Dora who looked up from a stack of insurance forms and did not blink at the two of them, one still in pajama pants, whispering at the shelf of cold medicine as cover. Amelia did the talking at first, haltingly, testing the phrases from her training like new shoes. Emergency contraception. Unprotected sex, five days ago. Dora nodded and slid a small box across the counter, and then she said the thing that rearranged the whole night.

"The sooner you take it, the better it works," Dora said. "It works mainly by delaying ovulation, so once the egg is already released, you've missed the window. Five days is really pushing it."

Priya stared at the box. "You mean waiting was the mistake."

"Waiting is always the mistake," Dora said, with the mild cheer of someone who has said this four hundred times. She rang it up without ceremony, mentioned that it didn't protect against infections, and told them the clinic on Delancey Street did testing on walk-in afternoons, no appointment, bring a book because the waiting room was slow. Then she said, "Next time, you come in the next morning," and turned back to her insurance forms as though the whole transaction had been about vitamins.

They sat on the curb outside the closed bakery next door while Priya swallowed the pill with warm water from Amelia's bottle, because Priya had refused to do it inside, in case the pharmacist watched, in case the pharmacist thought something. "She was thinking about her forms," Amelia said. "You could have juggled the box and she'd have stayed neutral."

"She was kind, though."

"She was kind, though," Amelia agreed. Priya leaned back on her hands and finally exhaled, and Amelia found herself doing the arithmetic she could not do out loud: that the pill might work and might not, that five days was five days, that neither of them would know anything for weeks. She had a training session on Saturday about exactly this, about how to tell a frightened freshman the same things Dora had said, and she realized she had learned more in twelve minutes at a pharmacy counter than in three Tuesdays with the binder. There was something funny about that, and also something that made her jaw tighten.

"So the clinic," Priya said. "Testing, Saturday, she said?"

"Walk-in afternoons. Bring a book."

Priya nudged her with an elbow. "You'll come with me. You can practice your whole peer educator machination on the receptionist."

"It's not a machination, it's a public service."

"With a sticker on the binder."

They walked toward the bus stop, and Amelia texted her grandmother that she'd be late, offering no explanation at all.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
Victoria had promised her cousin Dana the last of the lemon cake, and Dana arrived with the tin still warm from her own oven, so there were now two cakes on the kitchen table and one novel between them. The novel was Gone Girl, which Victoria had finished at one in the morning three days earlier, and which Dana had finished an hour before walking over. They had decided this in July, when the pool was still open and the plan had seemed far away: a book club with a membership of two, meeting at whichever house had the kitchen to itself.

"I feel stupid," Dana said, cutting the cake with more force than it needed. "I believed her. The whole diary part, I believed every word." She set the knife down and looked at Victoria the way she looked at referees who had made a bad call. "That's not fair. You can't just lie to the reader like that."

Victoria pulled two mugs from the cabinet and filled the kettle. "I believed it too," she said. "Until the middle."

"You didn't." Dana's voice went peevish, the tone she used when losing at cards. "You never believe anybody. You didn't believe Mrs. Halloran when she said the field trip money was going to buses."

"That was different. That was adults and money." Victoria carried the mugs to the table. "This was a diary. Diaries are supposed to be where you tell the truth when nobody's watching. That's the whole point of them."

She had been thinking about this since three in the morning, lying awake with the window cracked, listening to the neighbor's wind chimes. The book alternated between two narrators, husband and wife, and one of them, Amy, had kept a diary that turned out to be false, written deliberately to mislead the police. The novel had come out in 2012, four years before either of them could read it, and Victoria had found herself wondering how many readers across all those years had sat exactly here, in kitchens like this one, feeling exactly this betrayal.

Here was the question she could not let go of: had the author tricked Dana, or had Dana tricked herself? Because the diary chapters were not exactly lies. They were a performance of a person, the way Dana performed confidence at tryouts, or the way Victoria performed indifference when her essays came back with comments. The words on the page were true to something, just not to what they claimed to be true to.

"Okay," Victoria said, turning her mug a quarter turn on the table, a habit her mother called fidgeting and she called thinking. "When you read the husband's chapters, did you trust him?"

Dana considered, stealing the larger slice of cake for herself. "Halfway. He was hiding something about her, but I thought it was guilt, not, you know." She waved the fork. "So no. I didn't trust either of them, really. But the diary felt different."

"Why?"

"Because it was private. Because nobody writes lies in their own diary for themselves."

Victoria felt the small exhilaration of a door swinging open. "Except she wasn't writing it for herself. Once you know the diary is aimed at the police, it's not a diary anymore, it's evidence dressed up as a diary. It's wearing a costume." She reached across the table and slid the book toward Dana, open to the page she had dog-eared at two in the morning. "Look at this entry. She mentions the date, the weather, what he said. All checkable things. The lie isn't in the facts, it's in what the facts are arranged to make you feel."

Dana read the page with her fork suspended in the air. The kettle climbed toward a whistle behind them and Victoria got up to lift it off the burner before it sounded, because her father was asleep after a night shift and the house ran on small accommodations like that. She poured the water slowly, watching it steam.

"So the trick," Dana said slowly, "is that we trust the form, not the person. A diary gets trust just by being a diary."

"Or," Victoria said, sitting back down, "the narrator gets trust by borrowing it from the form. I can't decide which way to say it. Both feel true." She wrapped both hands around her mug. "And I don't know if that makes the book unfair or if it makes it honest, because people do walk around constructing themselves like that. I do it. You do it at tryouts."

Dana was quiet for a moment, chewing. "Then how am I supposed to know who to trust in a book? Or anywhere?"

"I don't think you're supposed to know," Victoria said. "I think you're supposed to notice why you trusted them in the first place." She took a bite of the cake Dana had baked, which was better than her own, and said so. Dana took the compliment with visible satisfaction, then closed the book and pushed it back across the table, cover up, the two faces on the jacket staring at the ceiling.

"We're reading something happy next," Dana said. "I mean it. Something with a dog in it."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
story:
The marble staircase inside city hall smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Keira climbed it two steps at a time with a folder of index cards against her chest. In the council chamber on the second floor, the folding tables had been pushed into a horseshoe, and a retired judge named Ms. Okafor sat at the top curve with a timer she had not yet turned over. Eight students had signed up for the summer mock court program, and in two weeks they would argue a real Supreme Court case before an audience of parents and city council members. The case involved a student who had been suspended for a banner he unfurled at a school event, and the question was whether the school could punish speech that happened to be offensive but not dangerous.

"Today," Ms. Okafor said, "you learn the hardest thing lawyers learn. You will argue the side you are given, and then, without warning, you will switch."

She dealt out assignments like cards. Keira drew petitioner, the student's side, and felt an immediate relief so strong it embarrassed her. Of course the school was wrong. Of course a banner, however crude, was just words. She had spent three days of her vacation on this program because she wanted to be the kind of person who said so in public.

Before they could choose positions, Ms. Okafor made them recite the source text. The First Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1791, says Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech. A boy named Deshawn read it aloud from the handout, slowly, and then everyone read it together, and Keira noticed the words for the first time instead of skating over them. Congress shall make no law. Not principals. Not school boards. She sat with that for a second, then raised her hand.

"Schools aren't Congress," she said. "So how does it even apply?"

"Argue it," Ms. Okafor said, and turned the timer over.

Deshawn went first, for the school, calling the banner a contrivance designed to derail an event, and Keira listened with her arms folded until she caught herself and unfolded them. When her turn came she spoke about a marketplace of ideas, about the danger of letting officials decide which words are too coarse to tolerate, and she heard her own voice go certain and ringing, the voice she used when she already knew she was right.

Then Ms. Okafor said, "Switch."

Keira opened her mouth to object and found nothing there. She looked down at her notes, and the notes looked back at her like they belonged to someone else. Slowly, she began again. If the amendment restrains Congress, she said, then the hard question was not whether schools may punish speech but what the amendment even reaches, and whether treating a school as just another public forum was specious, since the state compels students to be there in a way no citizen is compelled to stand on a street corner. She was building the argument, hating it and building it, when she stumbled onto something she had not expected: the argument was not bad. The school's case was not a bully's case. It was a custodial case, about children a state forces into a room together, and it did not collapse when she pressed on it. It bent.

Time ran out mid-sentence and Ms. Okafor did not turn the timer again. She only said, "Ms. Reyes, which side will you take in two weeks?"

The chamber went quiet except for the hum of the ceiling fan. Deshawn was watching her. So was Priya, who had argued the student's side with real anger, whose brother had actually been suspended that spring for something he had written in a group chat, though Keira only learned that afterward, in the parking lot, when Priya told her while unlocking her bike. In the moment itself, Keira knew only that the question had a shape like a trapdoor.

She thought about the amendment's words again, the exact ones she had recited, so absolute on the page and so slippery in a school hallway. She thought about Priya's face across the horseshoe, which she could not stop reading now as a face with something behind it. She thought about her own certain voice, which she suddenly did not trust.

"I don't know yet," Keira said.

"That's allowed," Ms. Okafor said. "It's the first honest thing anyone's said all afternoon."

Outside on the wide granite steps, the afternoon had gone gold, and Deshawn caught up with her and asked, "So are you going to problematize free speech for the audience, or actually pick?" She laughed, then didn't. Down at the curb, Priya was standing over her bike without getting on it, looking up at the two of them.

"Priya," Keira called. "Do you want to trade sides?"

Priya looked at her for a long moment, one hand still on the handlebars.

"Come say that closer," Priya said.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
story:
The tutoring centre smelled of dry-erase marker and the cheap hot chocolate that Mr. Davalos kept in a tin he maligne­d constantly, complaining it tasted like cardboard, while refilling his mug anyway. Sienna slid her quiz across the table. "Question four," she said. "He circled my answer and wrote see me, which is the scariest two words in the English language."

Priya, a second-year student who tutored on Tuesdays, pulled the paper closer and read. "You found the maximum," she said, "of that cubic on the interval from zero to six."

"I found where the derivative equals zero." Sienna tapped her work, the whole tidy line of it: the polynomial differentiated, the critical point solved for, the value calculated, the box drawn around the answer. "Three and a half. I even checked the second derivative to be sure it was a peak and not a valley. I did everything."

Priya turned the quiz face down on the table, which felt, in the fluorescent quiet of the centre, like a card being hidden mid-game. "Do it again," she said. "Same function. But this time, before you box anything, tell me what the function equals at zero and at six."

The centre around them carried on: an obstreperous boy two tables over arguing that his physics teacher had invented vectors purely to ruin his life, a girl whispering French verbs into her sleeve. Sienna wrote. She plugged in zero, got two. She plugged in six, got eleven. Her critical point, the peak she had been so proud of, the thing she had pounced on like the answer owed her money, gave four. She sat back.

"Eleven," she said. "The endpoint beats my beautiful peak by seven whole units." In October, during the unit on quadratics, her math teacher had drawn a parabola on the board and said its vertex was the whole story, the beginning and end of optimization, and Sienna had believed him the way you believe a map of a country you've never visited. Every graph since then had been, in her mind, a single hill with a single summit. "So my peak wasn't the maximum at all. It was just the biggest thing in the middle."

"Just the biggest thing in the middle," Priya repeated, pleased, as though Sienna had coined something for a T-shirt. She drew a quick sketch, a wiggling curve climbing and falling, and bracketed the ends of it with two vertical strokes like goalposts. "On a closed interval, the largest value can happen at an endpoint, where the derivative isn't zero. So the endpoints have to be checked too." She capped the pen. "That's it. That's the whole fact you lost four marks over."

"I lost four marks," Sienna said slowly, "because I trusted the middle of the story and never read the ending." She thought of her mother, who had a way of deciding how an evening would go based on the first ten minutes of it, and how often the last ten minutes proved her wrong, and how neither of them ever went back to check. She wasn't going to say that out loud. She flipped the quiz over again, took out a fresh pencil, and rewrote question four from the top: differentiate, solve, and then, in a new line she underlined twice, evaluate at both endpoints, compare, choose. The structure of it satisfied her, each step like a rung on a ladder she could actually climb.

"Quiz is Thursday," she said, packing up. Mr. Davalos was rinsing his mug, muttering at the hot chocolate tin again, and the boy with the vectors had moved on to blaming his English teacher for the existence of symbolism. Sienna zipped her bag and paused. "Here's what I still don't get, though. How do you know when you've checked enough? Endpoints, critical points, what else is hiding out there?" Priya only smiled and shrugged, which was the tutor's version of a cliffhanger.

On Thursday, question six was a polynomial on an interval from one to five, and Sienna, before finding a single peak, wrote down both endpoints in the margin like names on a list of suspects. Then she went back and found her critical point anyway, because the middle of the story still mattered, even if it no longer got to be the ending. When she handed the paper in, her teacher was already writing see me on somebody else's quiz, and Sienna slid hers onto the pile face up.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
The printout of Frida Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird lay on the picnic table, pinned at two corners by her mother's mason jars, and Jasmine had been staring at it for twenty minutes without writing a word. The assignment was due Monday: a formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism, and Professor Anand had been blunt about what she did not want, which was biography dressed up as criticism. Jasmine had already crossed out three opening sentences on the bus home. Behind her, her grandfather watered the tomato plants at the back fence, moving down the row with the unhurried attention he gave to everything.

She started with what she could see, making herself be systematic. The background was a wall of tropical leaves, dense and vertical, crowded with monkey faces and a black cat with lamp-yellow eyes. The figure sat dead centre, frontal and unmoving, so that everything green pressed inward on her. Thorns circled the throat and dug into the skin, and blood traced thin lines down toward the collar. Below, on a root at the lower left, sat a purple butterfly with outspread wings, and in the middle of her forehead, between the famous brows, a single fuchsia ribbon hung like a third eye. Jasmine wrote leaves press in, figure anchors, wrote diagonal of blood, and then stopped at the thing she could not account for.

The hummingbird. Black, wings folded, hanging dead from the thorn necklace at the throat, exactly where a pendant would rest. She had written it down as a symbol of something fragile, something about the weight of sorrow worn at the heart, and it had sounded fine until she read it aloud and heard how much she was guessing. She could describe the bird's placement precisely: the darkest value in the whole painting, dead centre vertically, swinging just below the chin. But she could not say what it meant, and Professor Anand would circle the sentence and write source? in the margin the way she had done twice already this term.

Her grandfather pulled a tomato off the vine, turned it over, set it in his basket, and wandered over to refill his watering can at the spigot. "That's the one with the bird," he said, glancing at the table. He had grown up in Jalisco and kept a small altar in the hallway with a picture of the Virgin and a strip of papel picado. Jasmine slid the printout toward him.

"That's a dead hummingbird," she said. "I can't figure out if I'm supposed to read it as morbid or what."

He bent closer, and something opened in his face, not sadness exactly but recognition. "We used to see those in the market when I was a boy," he said. "A dead hummingbird, worn at the throat. In Mexican folk tradition it's a charm for luck in love." He tapped the paper once, near Kahlo's chin. "Not just decoration."

Jasmine wrote the words down before she could lose them, then looked up. "Luck in love. From a dead bird."

"That's the paradox, isn't it," he said, and went back to his tomatoes.

She sat with that for a while, the hose hissing behind her, and the more she looked the more the painting seemed organised around exactly that paradox. The thorns that wounded were a necklace, an ornament. The blood was rendered carefully, almost decoratively, like the ribbon of silk at the brow. Kahlo had composed the image as a portrait of composure, frontal and symmetrical, and then hung the contradictory object at its dead centre, so that the eye kept returning to it the way the thorn necklace returned the viewer to the wound. It was not a symbol standing for sorrow the way she had first lazily assumed. It was a charm and a corpse at once, and the painting held both without resolving them. She thought of Professor Anand saying that formal analysis was not about decoding but about describing precisely enough that the contradictions became visible. The exhilaration of it surprised her, a physical lift in the chest, like the first day she had understood a proof in geometry.

She drafted fast for an hour, the paragraphs coming almost faster than her pen, and then she did the harder thing. She reread what she had written and crossed out half. The section on the cat and the monkey still felt thin; she did not know whether the black cat signified bad luck here or was simply Kahlo's own pet, and she could not pretend otherwise. So she kept the uncertainty, wrote that the animals frame the figure but that their symbolism resists a single reading, and decided that honesty about the limits of her evidence was worth more than a tidy paragraph. There was a kind of symbiosis, she thought, between what a painting showed and what a writer could responsibly claim about it, each one feeding the other only when neither tried to swallow the other whole.

By late afternoon the light had gone long and sedimentary, layering gold over the fence boards and the jars and the printout. Her grandfather came to sit at the picnic table with two glasses of agua de jamaica, red as the blood lines in the painting, and he read her final paragraph slowly, the way he read everything.

"Luck in love," he said, setting the paper down. "She painted it hanging dead."

"I know," Jasmine said. She folded the printout along the crease she had made on the bus, careful not to bend the bird. "That's the whole critique, really. I just have to say it right."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
The community garden behind the shuttered Lutheran school had forty plots and, by July, about eleven gardeners, which meant Noemie could spread her flashcards across two overturned milk crates without anyone asking her to share the bench. She had taken the plot for the tomatoes, honestly, and for the excuse to be somewhere her mother could not hand her a broom. The biochemistry textbook had followed her out of the house like a stray.

Glycolysis she could manage. Glucose, six carbons, split into two three-carbon sugars, a small profit of ATP taken upfront like a cover charge. It was after that the steps went soft in her mind. Pyruvate slipped into the mitochondria, the Krebs cycle turned, NADH crowded the electron transport chain, and then, at the end of all of it, ATP. She knew the order the way she knew the order of presidents: well enough for a quiz, not well enough to explain to a person.

Ms. Adeyemi from plot twelve was a retired lab technician who grew serrano peppers and regarded Noemie's flashcards with the fond contempt of someone who had once titrated solutions for a living. "You write it like a recipe," she said, watering Noemie's tomatoes without having been asked. "Step one, step two. Cells don't read recipes."

"How do they know what to do, then?" Noemie said, mostly to be polite.

"They don't know anything. They're chemistry. It just goes." Ms. Adeyemi pinched off a sucker branch. "The knowing is your problem."

That was Tuesday. On Thursday a boy named Teodoro, who was seventeen and worked his grandmother's plot with the seriousness of a man running a port, looked over her shoulder at the flashcard she'd propped against the fence. He was repeating twelfth grade, which he mentioned often, and which Noemie had decided not to hold against him. "ATP," he read. "That's the energy one, right? Like, the battery."

"The currency," Noemie said. "That's what the book calls it. The energy currency of the cell."

"Currency," Teodoro repeated, as though tasting it. "So somebody makes money in there. Like a mint."

She had meant to say that the metaphor was imperfect, that currency was only an analogy, but the image stayed with her on the bus home, a mint inside every cell, and that night, instead of rereading the chapter, she typed the enzyme's name into her phone. ATP synthase, the book said, made the ATP. What she found first was not a diagram but an announcement: Paul Boyer and John Walker had shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.

She read the sentence three times. Two men, a prize, for one enzyme. She thought of Ms. Adeyemi saying it just goes, and of the Nobel committee apparently disagreeing, disagreeing enough to give out a medal for figuring out how.

On Saturday she brought her phone to the garden, sat on the crates, and watched a video of the enzyme turning. It rotated. It actually rotated, a lopsided blob of a protein spinning like a motor, and each rotation squeezed out ATP the way her grandfather's old pasta machine squeezed out dough. She held the screen out to Teodoro. "Look. It spins."

Teodoro looked for a long moment. "It's making money," he said. "It's literally printing."

"And these two guys got the Nobel Prize for figuring that out. Nineteen ninety-seven." She said it flatly, still not quite believing the sentence. "Paul Boyer and John Walker. They shared it. For explaining how this thing makes ATP."

"For that?" Teodoro said. "For a little fan?" But he leaned closer. "Show me again where it spins."

Ms. Adeyemi came over with her watering can and stood behind them, saying nothing, which for her was a kind of applause. When the video ended she said, "In my lab we ordered that enzyme like flour. Ten dollars a vial. Nobody knew it spun."

"Does it matter?" Noemie asked. "If it works either way. If the cell doesn't need to know."

Ms. Adeyemi considered the tomatoes, which were coming in small and stubborn and would not be ready for weeks. "The cell doesn't," she said. "You do. That's the difference between you and your tomatoes, and it's not a large one, but it's real." She walked back to her peppers before Noemie could decide whether to be insulted.

Noemie sorted her flashcards. She had wanted, all summer, to reduce the pathway to something she could recite, glucose in, ATP out, an orderly mint. The truth she'd found was stranger: the cell ran a machine that spun, and it had taken two careers and a shared prize to say so, and somewhere under the recitation there was a question she could not close, which was whether understanding it was the same as needing it. She put glycolysis first, then the mitochondria, then ATP synthase, and on the synthase card, under the diagram, she wrote spins, and then, after a pause, 1997, Boyer and Walker, Nobel, and left it at that.

Teodoro was still watching the video, the little motor going around and around. "How fast do you think it spins?" he said. "Like, per second."

"Fast," Noemie said. "I don't know how fast. The card doesn't say." She picked up the hose and watered the tomatoes herself this time, and the leaves took the water the way they always had, needing to know nothing, while behind her Teodoro let the enzyme turn one more time.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
story:
The gallery closed at six, and Luca had until six to decide. He stood in the back room of the Hollis Street Art Space, where his AP class had been allowed to hang their work for one weekend, and looked at the ten pieces he had made over the year, all of them about hands doing work: his mother's hands kneading bread, his grandfather's hands on a fishing reel, his own hands failing at a knot, again and again, drawn in graphite until the smudge became the subject. Ten pieces, one theme, an artist's statement due Monday. That much he understood.

What he did not understand was the math. He had read the College Board page four times on his phone in the corner, thumbing past it as though the words would rearrange themselves into something kinder. The Selected Works section of the AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio asked for five artworks and counted for 40 percent of the score. Five. He had ten pieces that he loved in different ways, on different days, and the deadline for submitting was Monday at noon, and the gallery closed at six today, and his phone was at nine percent.

"You're pacing," said Priya, who had hung her own series of self-portraits along the west wall and was now sitting on a folding chair eating almonds from her coat pocket. "You've gone past the Monet print four times. It's not even a good print."

"I have to cut half of them," Luca said. "Five out of ten. And I can't tell if I'm supposed to pick the best five or the five that fit the statement I haven't written yet."

Priya considered this the way she considered most things, with her whole face. "Those might be different groups," she said. "That's actually a real problem." She held out the almonds. He took a handful and kept pacing.

His mother arrived at five with a thermos of coffee she had requisitioned from the bakery downstairs, along with two biscotti and an opinion. She walked the row of drawings slowly, her heels loud in the empty room, and stopped at the fourth one, the knot. "This one," she said. "The one where it's almost tied."

"It's not almost tied. That's the point. It's failing."

"It's trying," she said. "Put it in." She moved on to the bread drawing, the one Luca considered his strongest technically, the one his teacher had praised in October, and looked at it for a long moment without saying anything, which Luca had learned was how she criticized things.

The problem, once he said it out loud to Priya while his mother interrogated a volunteer about the gallery's heating, was that his technical best and his theme's best were not the same five. The bread drawing was beautiful and distant, a study in light. The knot drawing was clumsy and honest, a study in failure. If he submitted the five prettiest, his statement would have to be a lie about craft. If he submitted the five truest, two of them were the kind of thing a person had to stand in front of for a while to love, and the graders, he assumed, would not stand for a while.

"They spend like a minute," Priya said. "My cousin did this two years ago. She said they spend a minute, maybe less, per piece." Priya wanted to study chemistry and paint anyway, and Luca had once called her a polymath to annoy her, because she hated the word, and it had become their running joke. Tonight she didn't rise to it, which meant she could see he was actually scared.

He sat down on the floor between the eighth and ninth pieces, a self-portrait of his hands holding a pencil drawn with the wrong hand, and a drawing of his grandfather's hands on the reel, done from memory a week after the funeral. The self-portrait was funny, objectively funny, the line wobbling like a seismograph, and Priya had laughed at it in September in a way that had made him feel understood. The reel drawing was the one he could barely look at. He tried a sentence in his head: these works are about hands, which is to say about what people do with what they are given. Too neat. He tried again: I drew hands because faces ask to be read and hands only show. Worse.

"Sixty percent of the score is the other section," Priya said, reading over his shoulder at the College Board page, "so the five you pick are worth less than everything else you've already done. It's forty percent. You're agonizing over the smaller half." Luca looked at his phone, which was now at four percent, and at his mother, who was standing in front of the knot drawing again with her arms crossed, and at the reel drawing, and something rearranged itself in him, not into certainty but into a decision made with the uncertainty still in it. The forty percent was not the smaller half of the problem. The forty percent was five pieces, and five was a number he could hold in his head and defend, one at a time, if anyone asked.

"Okay," he said, getting up. "Bread, knot, reel, pencil, and the one of your hands." Priya blinked. The last piece, hung at the end of the row, was a study he had done in March of her hands holding the almond tin from the sculpture room, which she had stolen back from the ceramics teacher in a small act of art-world crime he had witnessed and she had denied for a week.

"That's not even about work," she said. "That's about theft."

"Your hands were working," Luca said. He pulled the five drawings off the wall while his mother took down the others and rolled them with the gallery's tape, and he photographed each one on the clean gray floor by the window while there was still light, kneeling, phone trembling at three percent, two, one. "The statement will say the theme is hands," he said to Priya, who was holding the curtain back for the last shot. "Everything after that, I'm still figuring out."

"Write that," she said. "I'm serious. Write that."

story:
Marcus's eighteenth was in his backyard, string lights and a playlist somebody's older sister had curated, and Cole had been carrying the same sentence around for an hour without saying it. The sentence was about Priya. They were co-captains of the debate team, and at the last tournament her closing rebuttal had collapsed into a soft, apologetic summary, and he had told her afterward that it was "solid," which it had not been. He'd been telling himself all week that he was sparing her feelings. He was starting to suspect he was sparing himself the conversation.

"I'm not a liar," he said to Ren, who was sitting on the cooler because all the chairs were taken. "I just didn't say the whole truth."

Ren was in his psych class, the one Cole had taken only because it fit his schedule. "That's a distinction," Ren said, and popped a soda. Somewhere behind them Marcus was failing to light the candles in the wind.

"She thinks we lost on judges' bias. We lost because her rebuttal had nothing in it." Cole had watched the round from the back of the room, arms crossed, cataloguing everything wrong with what she was doing, and then had walked up afterward and praised her transitions. Transitions. He had praised the connective tissue of a speech that had no organs.

"Freshman year my English teacher wrote all over my essay," Ren said. "Brutal stuff. I actually revised it, though, which I never did before." Cole asked why, and Ren shrugged. "At the end she'd added this note. In a 2014 study David Yeager ran, students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. She told us that was why she bothered writing the belief part. So she wrote it." He drained the can. "Worked on me, anyway."

Cole turned that over. It bothered him a little, the idea that belief needed to be stated out loud, that it was a technique. His father had operated on the opposite theory, that praise was inflation and criticism was the currency of respect, that saying I expect better and nothing else was itself a form of faith. An amalgam of the two approaches, Yeager's and his father's, seemed possible in principle: high standards, stated belief, specific criticism. What seemed less possible was Cole saying any of it to Priya's face, at a party, over cake.

"She's going to think I pathologize her," he said. "Like I've been psychoanalyzing her failures all season."

"Have you?"

"I've been noticing them."

"Same thing," Ren said, and laughed, and Cole laughed too, uneasily, because it was not entirely the same thing and he knew the difference, though he could not have sworn he'd always kept to the right side of it.

He found Priya by the fence, holding a cup she wasn't drinking, watching Marcus wrestle with a lighter. He had planned to wait until Monday, practice room, neutral territory. He heard himself say her name instead.

"I need to tell you something about the rebuttal, and I'm going to do it badly, so let me do it badly and then you can tell me what I got wrong." She turned, and her face did the thing it did before cross-examination, a kind of atavistic steadying, chin down, eyes up. He took a breath. "Your closing had no clash in it. You summarized our case instead of answering their two strongest points, the one about precedent and the one about cost. Both were answerable. I think you can answer them better than anyone on the circuit, and I think you folded because you didn't trust your own answers. I watched you do it and I said 'solid' after, and that was me being a coward, not you being fine."

Priya was quiet long enough that the candles finally caught, and everybody by the table cheered.

"You're telling me this at a birthday party," she said.

"I know."

"You couldn't have picked Monday."

"I believe you can beat Whitman next round," he said, "and I apparently believe it so much I couldn't wait two days."

She looked at him for a moment, then at her cup. "Say the Whitman part again Monday," she said. "At practice. Where I can yell at you." Then she walked toward the table to get cake before it was gone, and Cole stood by the fence realizing that the truest thing he'd said all night was the part he'd improvised.

He went to get cake too, and found Marcus in his way, holding out the knife. "Dude," Marcus said, grinning. "Did you just coach her? At my party?"

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
story:
Gavin locked the bathroom door, set his phone timer for three minutes, and faced the mirror. He had volunteered to co-lead the health workshop on Friday, and Ms. Reyes had emailed him a list of topics that included consent, contraception, and where to get tested for infections, as if the words themselves were simple objects he could hand to a room of sophomores. He pressed record on his phone and began.

"Consent is when someone says yes," he said, and stopped, because that wasn't right, was it? A yes could be bored, or tired, or frightened. He tried again. "Consent is a yes you can take back, anytime, and it has to be free, which means nobody's cornered you into giving it." His voice sounded thin in the small room, bouncing off the tile. He ran the tap to drown out the last attempt, then started over.

The timer buzzed. He sat down on the edge of the tub and pulled up the clinic's website on his phone. There was a student walk-in on Thursday afternoons, no appointment needed, and a line that said testing was free and confidential for anyone under eighteen. He wondered whether his classmates knew that, whether any of them had walked past the glass door with the blue decal and assumed it wasn't for people like them, whatever they thought people like them were.

On Thursday he went himself, partly out of curiosity and partly because it seemed fraudulent to stand up on Friday and describe a place he'd never entered. The waiting room had a rack of pamphlets fanned out like cards. He took one on contraception and read it in a plastic chair while a basketball game murmured on a wall-mounted TV. A girl from his chemistry class, Dana, was already there, and after a long, mutually awkward pause she said, "You can not tell anyone you saw me." He said, "Same," and something in the room got easier.

The nurse called him back and asked what he wanted to know. He admitted, feeling heat climb his neck, that he was supposed to explain contraception to thirty sophomores and didn't trust the pill diagram in the textbook. She opened a drawer of demonstration models and lined up options on the counter. "The pill works well if you take it every single day," she said, "and that's the problem. Real life happens." Then she held up a small T-shaped device and a matchstick-sized rod. "The hormonal IUD and the implant fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on daily use."

"So the implant's better in practice," Gavin said slowly, "not because it's stronger, but because it doesn't need you to remember." She nodded. He wrote it on his hand, then thought better of it and copied it into his phone. There was something almost elegant about it, the way the most reliable method was the one that asked the least, and he wanted to get the reasoning right, not just the statistic. He asked about testing, and she walked him through the swabs and the urine cup and the two-week wait for results, all of it routine, none of it shameful, and he felt the clinic enfranchise him in a way no assembly ever had.

Friday came, and the workshop was interminable in its first five minutes, his elocution stiff and rehearsed, until a kid in the back row asked, "What if she says yes but she looks scared?" Gavin put down his notes. He said he didn't have a rule for that, only a question you could ask out loud: are you sure? He said the clinic on Miller Street was open Thursdays and would see you alone. Then he held up his drawing of the implant, stick-figure arm and all, and repeated the numbers the nurse had given him, fewer than one in a hundred a year, no daily remembering required.

Afterward Dana caught him at the lockers. "You went Thursday," she said. "That's why you weren't weird about it." He hadn't worked out yet how much of his own uncertainty to show next time, whether honesty about what he didn't know was a strength or a confession. Dana zipped her bag and said, "Walk-in's Thursday again, right?" and he said, "Two o'clock," and held the door.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
story:
Oliver stood at the steel counter with a clipboard he did not want anyone to see him holding. Chef Rivas had assigned each of the second-year students a week of menus to plan, shop for, and cook in batches, and the clipboard was Oliver's way of pretending he had done this before. Around him the kitchen ran its evening rhythm, tickets snapping onto the rail, the fryer hissing, and at the far station his friend Dani cut peppers into strips so uniform they could have been printed. He wanted to be that calm. Instead he had forty servings of chili to portion, cool, and store before close, and a list of groceries for four more dinners that he had not yet priced.

"You're staring at the pot like it owes you money," Dani said, bringing him a ladle.

"I'm planning." He wasn't, exactly. He was transfixed by the steam rising off the chili in a slow rope, thinking about Sunday afternoons at his grandmother's house, where she would leave a pot of beans on the back porch overnight because her mother had done it that way in a kitchen with no refrigerator. He could still see the towel she draped over the lid, the porch light going dark, the beans waiting for morning like a small animal in a den. She had never once gotten sick. Or if she had, she had never said.

He portioned the chili into shallow hotel pans, slid them into the walk-in, and wrote the times on masking tape labels. Then, on Sunday night, in his own apartment with his housemate Theo, he did it differently, because he was tired and proud and wanted the kitchen to smell like the restaurant. They made a double batch for the week, ate bowls of it at eleven, and left the rest in the pot on the stove while they watched a movie. At one in the morning Oliver glanced toward the kitchen and thought, we should put it away. He thought it the way you think about flossing. He went to bed.

It was Theo who found him in the hallway at seven, holding his phone like evidence. "Is this pot still warm?" Theo asked. "Because my food safety app says leaving food out is how people get sick, and I have a midterm Thursday and cannot have food poisoning."

From where Theo stood, the whole thing looked like a small crime scene. The pot sat on the cold burner, a skin had formed across the surface, and the ladle leaned against the rim at the angle of something abandoned mid-thought. He had watched Oliver all week carry home totes of labeled containers, cool them properly, tape dates to lids, and he knew his housemate took the class seriously, which was why the pot bothered him. He searched the USDA page while Oliver was still rubbing sleep out of his eyes and read the numbers aloud.

"The USDA calls four to sixty degrees Celsius the danger zone," Theo said. "That's forty to one hundred forty Fahrenheit. The range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly."

Oliver felt the sentence land somewhere behind his ribs. He looked at the pot and did the arithmetic he had avoided doing at one in the morning: hours in that range, hours for multiplying. "So it's not tenable," he said slowly. "Serving it. Even reheating it."

"Reheating doesn't fix it, according to this. The stuff that grows, some of it makes toxins that heat doesn't destroy." Theo paused. "Sorry. I'm not trying to lecture. I just don't want either of us on the bathroom floor."

Oliver spooned the chili into the compost bag, all twelve cups of it, and stood there holding the empty pot under the tap. His grandmother's porch floated back to him, the covered beans, the generations of nobody dying, and he understood that both things could be true at once. Her method had probably worked for reasons she never named, a cold porch, a salt-heavy broth, luck compounding until it looked like tradition. The danger zone was not an argument against her; it was an explanation of the risk she had been running without a word for it. He thought of his epidemiology-obsessed cousin who liked tracing every illness to its etiology, its origin story, and realized that was what he was doing now, tracing his own mistake back through the evening to the moment he had decided that morning would be soon enough.

"Okay," he said. "New system." He pulled out his phone and made two lists, one for groceries, one for the steps between cooking and eating: cool it fast, shallow pans, straight into the fridge, everything down out of the danger zone before bed, no exceptions for tiredness or tradition. Theo watched over his shoulder and added "buy a second fridge thermometer" to the bottom, then made coffee without being asked and set a cup at Oliver's elbow.

They rebuilt the week on Wednesday, shopping together after Oliver's shift, Theo carrying the onions because Oliver's hands still smelled of bleach from scrubbing the pot. In the restaurant kitchen on Thursday, Dani found him at the steel counter with his clipboard, now covered edge to edge in times and temperatures, and picked it up without asking.

"Batch plan," Oliver said. "Cook Sunday, cool it right, portion Monday. Four dinners."

Dani read the top line, then looked at the walk-in where his labeled pans sat in a cold, orderly row. "Grandma's chili recipe?"

"Something like that," Oliver said, and taped the last label down flat with his thumb.
